name: Gareth Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Our crew looks after the lines up the valley, from the bottom village to the pass, and in winter it's snow and ice on the wires half the time. We start at the depot at seven, the foreman, Rhys, who's my brother-in-law, gives out the work, and off we go in the trucks. I'm still junior, so I'm on the ground, chaining the trucks, digging out the poles, hauling the gear, and learning to climb in the cold. I like being out in the hills and I like the men I work with, it's honest work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Rhys is your brother-in-law. How did you come to the job, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did twenty years at the quarry, cutting and loading stone, until it closed. Rhys put a word in for me and they took me on as an apprentice at forty, which I'm grateful for. The hard part is the theory, the exams, I'm a hands man, not a book man. And the money's tight, Karen cleans at the care home, we've got the mortgage and two kids, and there's barely anything left at the end of the month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, what did I tell you, it's all talk. At the depot we'd have a laugh, the lads always said a computer can't climb a pole in a blizzard. I'm not online much, Karen does the social media.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing changes, and that suits me down to the ground. I've got a job, a family, and Rhys looking out for me. I'd just like to get my ticket and keep this job till I retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as I am. Turn up, do the work, try to pass the next exam in March, though it's not my strong point. Maybe do a bit of extra on weekends, fixing fences for the farmers, for cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Steady. Nothing to fret about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any of these AI things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, never. I don't trust them. Owen uses something for his homework and I tell him, do it yourself, use your own head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So what's on your mind, if not that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The exam, honestly, and the boiler, which is on its last legs. And whether Karen gets her hours cut at the care home, which happens every winter.

S0.say: He'd say it was all talk and the crew would joke that a computer can't climb a pole in a blizzard. His wife handles the social media.
S0.think: Nothing changes, which suits me down to the ground. I've got a job, a family and my brother-in-law looking out for me.
S0.do: Keeps turning up and works toward his next exam in March. Does weekend fence repairs for farmers for extra cash.
S0.feel: Good and steady, nothing to fret about.
S0.quote: Owen uses something for his homework and I tell him, do it yourself, use your own head.
S0.fieldNote: Gareth distrusts AI and tells his son to use his own head. He's grateful to his brother-in-law for the job after the quarry closed. His worries are concrete and small: the exam, the boiler and his wife's winter hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it'll be the office lot who need to worry, not us up the valley. At work we'd say let them try sending a robot over the pass in February. I'd keep my head down and carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be a bit worried, because I'm the junior and I'm slow with the exams. But I don't think they'll bring robots up our valley any time soon, it's too rough. I'd wait and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on working, pass my exams, be useful. I wouldn't go on any computer courses, that's not me. I'd maybe keep doing the fence work on weekends for a bit extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but not much. More like a cloud on the hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of the job do you think would change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning, maybe, and the checking of lines from the air, they do that with helicopters already. But the actual work up the valley, I can't see it. You need a man who knows the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait. What if it does reach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd talk to Rhys, see what he thinks. And I'd look to family. My brother's a builder, he always needs a labourer. We look after our own.

S1.say: He'd say the office workers should worry, not the crews up the valley, and joke about sending a robot over the pass in February.
S1.think: I'd be a bit worried as the junior who's slow with exams, but robots won't come up our rough valley any time soon. I'd wait and see.
S1.do: Carries on working toward his exams and keeps the weekend fence work. Refuses computer courses and would turn to his brother-in-law and his builder brother if change reached him.
S1.feel: A little uneasy, like a cloud on the hill.
S1.quote: Let them try sending a robot over the pass in February.
S1.fieldNote: Gareth trusts the valley's rough ground to protect him and plans to wait. His safety net is family, not training: his brother-in-law and his builder brother. He rules out computer courses flatly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when we let a few big companies run everything without asking anybody. At the depot I'd say we look after each other, same as always. I'd tell Karen to post something about it, she's better at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be finished. I'm not good enough at this yet to be kept, I'm not good with computers, and there's nothing else in the valley since the quarry. Two years, we'd be in real trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sit down with Karen and cut everything but the mortgage and food. Ask my brother and Rhys if there's any work going, labouring, anything. If it came to it, ask Karen's mum if we could move in with her, she's got the old farmhouse. I'd ask the men at church too, they'd help where they could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked, if I'm honest. I don't see a way through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them their dad would work, whatever it took, and family sticks together. Owen's fourteen, he'd want to help, maybe get a paper round. Megan's ten, she'd just want to know if we're keeping the dog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to, for the kids. But I'd hate it. I've always worked, my father always worked, and I'd want it to be short.

S2.say: He'd blame a few big companies running everything without asking anyone and tell the crew to look after each other. He'd ask his wife to post about it.
S2.think: I'd be finished: not good enough yet to be kept, not good with computers, and nothing else in the valley since the quarry. Two years and we'd be in real trouble.
S2.do: Cuts everything but the mortgage and food with Karen and asks his brother and brother-in-law for any labouring work. Asks Karen's mother about moving into her farmhouse and leans on the men at church. Takes government help only reluctantly and briefly, for the kids.
S2.feel: Panicked, unable to see a way through.
S2.quote: I've always worked, my father always worked, and I'd want it to be short.
S2.fieldNote: With no savings, no other work in the valley and no wish to learn computers, Gareth sees no way through. He turns first to family and church, and accepts government help only for his children. He blames big companies, not workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough for people to get ready, if they've got any sense. At work I'd say keep your heads down and do good work. I'd not go on about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years means I'd get my ticket and have a few years of proper pay. But I'd still lose the job at the end, and I'd be forty-eight with nothing else to do. The valley won't have anything for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save what I can, even fifty a month, and do more weekend fence work. Cut back on the extras, the kids' clubs, the takeaways. And talk to my brother about learning the building trade properly, as a labourer first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, I'd say. It's a slow countdown, and I'd feel it every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I fall later, not that I don't fall. I'd have time to save a bit and maybe learn building from my brother. But it's still the end of the line, so to speak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you're not a book man. Would five years of warning change your mind about training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Building with my brother, maybe, because that's hands-on and he'd teach me. Computers, no, I'd be wasting everyone's time.

S3.say: He'd say five years is long enough to get ready if people have sense, and tell the crew to keep their heads down and do good work.
S3.think: I'd get my ticket and a few years of proper pay, but I'd still lose the job at 48 with nothing else in the valley.
S3.do: Saves even 50 a month, does more weekend fence work and cuts kids' clubs and takeaways. Talks to his brother about learning the building trade, starting as a labourer, while ruling out computer training.
S3.feel: Alarmed, a slow countdown felt every day.
S3.quote: It's a slow countdown, and I'd feel it every day.
S3.fieldNote: Five years delays Gareth's fall without changing it. He'd learn building from his brother, which fits his hands-on nature and his faith in family, but he won't touch computers. The countdown itself would weigh on him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, plenty can change. At work I'd say do your job well and the rest will sort itself out. I'd not lose sleep over it out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I'd get some good years out of this job, and the kids would be grown. But at fifty-three, I'd be done with no pension to speak of. I'd be relying on family and whatever work my brother could give me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working the lines and save what I can each month. Learn the building trade from my brother on weekends. And push Owen toward an apprenticeship in a trade that needs a man on site, plumbing maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but there's time to get used to it. Like a long winter you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years puts Owen and Megan into their twenties. Does that change things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. If Owen has a trade by then and Megan's settled, that's half my worry gone. Then it's just Karen and me, and we can manage on less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want Owen to follow you onto the lines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not now, no. I'd want him to have something steady, plumbing or building, where a man's hands are needed. I'd hate to see him start on something that's ending.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is a long time and plenty can change, and tell the crew to do their jobs well and the rest will sort itself out.
S4.think: I'd get some good years out of the job and the kids would be grown, but at 53 I'd be done with no pension to speak of, relying on family and my brother's work.
S4.do: Keeps working the lines and saves what he can each month. Learns the building trade from his brother on weekends and steers his son toward a plumbing apprenticeship.
S4.feel: Anxious, but with time to get used to it, like a long winter he knows is coming.
S4.quote: I'd hate to see him start on something that's ending.
S4.fieldNote: The decade matters to Gareth mostly through his children: if they're settled, half his worry is gone. He steers his son away from line work and toward a hands-on trade. He still expects to rely on family rather than retraining or public support.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no doubt. What would help is the company keeping on the men who've given them good years, or at least giving a proper payout and a reference. And proper apprenticeships in trades that still need hands, paid, not some computer course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the valleys. Everyone thinks about the cities. Up here, when the quarry closed, half the young men left. If the lines go too, there'll be nobody left but the old and the sheep.

headlineQuote: If the lines go too, there'll be nobody left but the old and the sheep.
portrait: Gareth Rahman is a 43-year-old junior lineworker on a mountain valley crew, who came to the trade at 40 after twenty years at a quarry that closed, with his brother-in-law Rhys putting in a word. His partner Karen cleans at a care home, they have two kids and a mortgage, and there's barely anything left each month. He never uses AI, trusts family and church over government, and blames big companies for running things without asking. He is calm when AI stalls, a little uneasy about gradual change, panicked at AGI in two years, alarmed at five, and anxious at ten, when he pins his hopes on his children having trades.
whatWouldHelp: The company keeping on men who've given good years, or at least a proper payout and a reference, plus paid apprenticeships in trades that still need hands.
